question.problem:
The function $f(x)$ is given by

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}{log}_{3}⁡3(x-k), & x\ne 1, \\ 2, & x=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=1,$ what is the value of $k?$
question.worked_solution:
From the definition of $f(x),$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to 1}{log}_{3}⁡3(x-k) \\  & ={log}_{3}⁡3(1-k).\end{aligned}
$$

In order for $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x=1,$ we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}f(x) & =f(1) \\ {log}_{3}⁡3(1-k) & =2 \\ 3(1-k) & ={3}^{2} \\ 1-k & =3 \\ k & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, setting $k=-2$ removes the point discontinuity.
